text: Set operations — stacking two queries together and comparing their result sets — are mostly standard across every dialect in this course. This lesson covers all three: union, intersect, and the operator that returns rows in one query but not the other, which has exactly one real naming split you need to memorize. Everything else here is good news.

UNION and UNION ALL have no surprises at all, on any platform. Select customer id from ActiveCustomers, union, select customer id from ArchivedCustomers — that combines both result sets and removes duplicates. Swap in UNION ALL and duplicates are kept instead. This is written character-for-character the same way on T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL. There is nothing here to unlearn or relearn.

INTERSECT is standard too — it returns only the rows present in BOTH queries. Select customer id from OnlineOrders, intersect, select customer id from StoreOrders, gives you customers who ordered both online and in-store. T-SQL, Oracle, and PostgreSQL have all supported this for a long time. MySQL is the newest to the party here — more on that in a moment.

Now the one real naming difference in this entire lesson. The operator that returns rows from the first query that do NOT appear in the second: T-SQL, PostgreSQL, and modern MySQL all call it EXCEPT, which is also the ANSI-standard name. Oracle alone calls the exact same operation MINUS. Same semantics — customers in the first set, absent from the second — completely different keyword. Try to write EXCEPT against an Oracle database and you'll get a syntax error; Oracle has simply never adopted that keyword, even though it's the standard name everywhere else.

One more detail worth knowing: MySQL is the newest adopter of this whole family of operators. INTERSECT and EXCEPT were only added in MySQL version 8.0.31. Anything earlier — older 8.0 releases, or MySQL 5.7 and before — supports only UNION and UNION ALL. If you need the same logic on an older MySQL version, you simulate INTERSECT or EXCEPT with a JOIN or a NOT EXISTS subquery instead.

To sum up: UNION and UNION ALL are fully portable everywhere. INTERSECT is standard on T-SQL, Oracle, and PostgreSQL, and arrived on MySQL in 8.0.31. And the one name to memorize: three platforms call it EXCEPT, Oracle calls the identical operation MINUS. Next lesson closes out this chapter with genuinely good news: window functions, one of the most portable and standardized areas of modern SQL across every dialect in this course.
